Cover: Velocity tells how fast something moves and in which direction. Watch for two ways it can change: a car can speed up or it can turn.
How this lesson works: Before a reveal, the lead reads the problem. Everyone tries it. The scribe shows the steps so the group can compare ideas.
Today's learning target: Start with two speeds in the same direction. If a bike goes from 3 to 5 m/s in one second, its velocity gains 2 m/s in that second.
The asteroid thread: Picture the asteroid moving straight ahead. If gravity pulls it sideways, its path bends. That turn is a change in velocity.
What's its acceleration?: Read the starting speed, then the ending speed. Find the gain and divide it by the seconds. For now, say the gain in mph each second.
Watch the gaps grow: Trace the dots from left to right. Each gap took the same time. A wider gap means the object went farther in that time, so it moved faster.
A velocity graph tells the change: Read across for time and up for velocity. Move one second to the right. The line rises by 2 m/s each time, so the change is steady.
How fast does velocity change?: Start at the first velocity and count up to the last one. That gap is the total gain. Divide the gain by the time before you reveal the answer.
Acceleration: The triangle means change. For velocity, subtract the start from the end. Divide by the time that passed to get the average change each second.
What changes each second?: Read the notebook in the panel. A scooter at 4 m/s has a velocity if you also know its direction. To find acceleration, you need to know how its velocity changes over time.
Compare to gravity: The car starts at rest. After the unit change, its gain is 27 m/s in 6 seconds. Divide to get 4.5 m/s each second. Compare that rate with free fall.
Imagine a bike rolling right as you squeeze the brakes. It still moves right, but it loses some rightward velocity each second. Its acceleration points left.
One step at a time: First find what was added. The cart already had 2 m/s at the start. Take that away from 6 m/s at the end. The gain is 4 m/s.
Share the change across time: Now spread that gain over the two seconds. With a steady gain, the velocity goes from 2 to 4 to 6 m/s. Each step adds the same amount.
Acceleration measures velocity change: Think of velocity as an arrow. Its length shows speed. Its tip points where the object goes. A change in either one means the object accelerates.
Speeding up, slowing down, or constant?: Read each line from left to right. A line rising above zero means the object is gaining speed in the positive direction. A flat line means its velocity stays the same.
Read the slope, not the height: Put your finger at the start of the graph. Move to the last point. Divide the rise in velocity by the time you moved across. That rate is the slope.
Equations of motion: Choose the equation by what you want to find. For final velocity, multiply steady acceleration by time. Add that change to the velocity you had at the start.
Braking is acceleration too: Draw two arrows pointing right, one for each velocity. Make the second arrow shorter. Use the arrows to explain what changed while the cart kept moving right.
Direction matters: Trace a turn with your finger. Pause twice and point the way the car is moving. Your finger points in different directions even if the speed stays the same.
Keep the start velocity: Follow the cart in the panel. It starts at 2 m/s and gains 3 m/s each second. After 4 seconds the gain is 12 m/s. Add the start to find the final velocity.
Earth’s pull at the starting separation: Read r as the distance between the centers of Earth and the asteroid. Use meters in the formula. The result tells how much Earth alone changes the asteroid’s velocity each second at that distance.
Gravity changes along the path: Look at the distance in the bottom of the gravity formula. A smaller distance makes the pull stronger. Recheck the distance before using the same acceleration later.
A small change is still a change: Follow the estimate in the panel: multiply the change each second by the number of seconds. This works if the pull stays steady. Over a long trip, both distance and pull can change.
Signs describe directions: Read across one row at a time. When velocity and acceleration point the same way, the object speeds up. When they point opposite ways, it slows down until it stops or the acceleration changes.
Your turn: one calculation: Write the ending velocity minus the starting velocity on the top line. Put the elapsed time below it. Divide, then check that your unit tells how velocity changes each second.
Negative does not mean slow: Use zero as the stop point on a number line. For a negative velocity, getting closer to zero means slowing down. Moving farther from zero means speeding up.
Braking in the positive direction: Mark the car’s starting velocity and place its ending velocity at zero. Trace from start to end to decide the sign of the change. Then divide by the braking time.
Braking in the negative direction: Put both negative velocities on a number line. Follow the arrow from the first to the second. Use the arrow’s direction for the sign of the change before you divide.
Exit ticket · on your own: Work on your own. Choose a positive direction and write down the start, end, and time. Show your subtraction and division. Read your sign back in words before you turn it in.
